classification.text: “Could we agree on what the task is asking us to accomplish?”
classification.why: This clarifies the task so the group shares a starting point.

classification.text: “A recent study found that students receiving counseling had improved attendance.”
classification.why: This introduces evidence relevant to the issue.

classification.text: “We have about 15 minutes remaining, so we should begin narrowing our recommendations.”
classification.why: This manages time and focuses the group.

classification.text: “I think we can combine those two proposals into one stronger recommendation.”
classification.why: This synthesizes ideas into a potential solution.

classification.text: “Our discussion seems to be moving away from the problem described in the task.”
classification.why: This redirects the group toward its assigned task.

analysisAnswers.who: Members of the American School Counselor Association, developing a plan counselors could implement.
analysisAnswers.what: The negative effects of mental health stigma on K-12 students.
analysisAnswers.how: Examine the effects of stigma and craft a plan for counselors to implement.
analysisAnswers.where: National convention setting; solutions implemented in K-12 schools.
analysisAnswers.terms: American School Counselor Association; mental health stigma; K-12 students; effects of stigmatization.

options: The negative effects of mental health stigma on K-12 students.
Craft a plan counselors can implement in their schools.
whatHow.explanation: WHAT names the central problem. Crafting a plan is HOW: the action and deliverable.

options: A. Begin brainstorming programs immediately.
B. Clarify the problem and the task's required deliverable.
C. Vote on who should lead the discussion.
clarification.explanation: The group should agree on what the task requires before deciding how to organize its time.

options: A. Restart all clarifications.
B. Ignore the student's concern without discussion.
C. Ask whether a specific misunderstanding needs resolving, then share relevant research.
research.explanation: Check for a specific new misunderstanding; if there is none, move into useful background and evidence.

options: Asking the group to clarify the task
Introducing research about an issue's effects
Suggesting a time limit
quiz.explanation: Research introduces evidence and develops the discussion's content.

quiz.prompt: Which opening sequence is in the right order?
options: Read → Analyze → Clarify → Establish direction → Research
Read → Set agenda → Clarify → Research
Research → Establish direction → Read → Clarify
quiz.explanation: Understand and clarify the task before setting direction; research follows.

quiz.prompt: In task analysis, what is the difference between WHAT and HOW?
options: WHAT is a source; HOW is a citation.
WHAT is the central problem; HOW is the required action or deliverable.
WHAT is the setting; HOW is the assigned role.
quiz.explanation: WHAT names the problem. HOW names what the group needs to do about it.

quiz.prompt: What is the purpose of clarifications?
options: To debate solutions before reading
To choose a permanent leader
To agree on the role, problem, required actions, and deliverable
quiz.explanation: Clarification builds shared understanding before the group debates solutions.

quiz.prompt: How do an agenda and a consensus question differ?
options: An agenda is a roadmap; a consensus question defines the destination.
An agenda states the problem; a consensus question sets speaking order.
They are identical and both require fixed time limits.
quiz.explanation: An agenda organizes stages; a consensus question identifies what the group should accomplish.

classification.q: “We have about 15 minutes left. Should we move to evaluating solutions?”
classification.feedback: This manages time and discussion structure.

classification.q: “A report on transportation access could help us assess participation barriers.”
classification.feedback: This introduces research relevant to the problem. An actual contribution should cite its publication and date.

classification.q: “Before moving on, does anyone have another perspective?”
“Combining transportation and outreach could address two barriers at once.”
classification.feedback: This develops a solution by connecting proposals.

classification.q: “Our conversation is drifting away from the task.”

research.text: “Transportation matters. I have seen that myself.”
research.feedback: A personal observation does not use the available research.

research.text: “According to the fictional Community Access Survey from May 2025, 38% of surveyed students reported missing at least one after-school activity because of transportation difficulties. We should consider whether transportation support could improve participation.”
research.feedback: This identifies the source and date, describes the fictional finding, and connects it to a possible solution.

research.text: “I found a transportation statistic, but we should discuss a different issue.”
research.feedback: Research is less useful when it derails the conversation.

research.text: “The survey proves transportation is the only barrier.”
research.feedback: The survey does not establish that transportation is the only barrier.

group.title: The quiet tablemate
group.q: Several students have contributed little. The group is about to move on.
options: “Jordan, you need to talk more.”
“Before we move on, are there any additional perspectives?”
“We have heard enough.”
group.feedback: A broad invitation encourages participation without putting one person on the spot.

group.title: The detour
group.q: The transportation discussion has drifted into a long debate about lunch menus.
options: “That has nothing to do with anything.”
“Let’s keep discussing lunch.”
“Could we return to the transportation barriers our plan needs to address?”
group.feedback: Respectfully return to the task and offer a way forward.

group.title: The clock
group.q: Limited time remains, and the proposed plan is unfinished.
options: “Could we prioritize recommendations and reserve time to review the plan?”
“I will decide the plan.”
“Time does not matter.”
group.feedback: Time management helps the group finish without taking over its decisions.

options: Roll your eyes while taking notes.
Keep a neutral expression and explain your concern respectfully.

communication.q: You are making a point in a noisy gym.
options: Maintain clear volume through the final words.
Let your voice fade before finishing.
communication.feedback: An audible ending helps others hear your complete thought.

communication.q: You are playing a city advisory committee member.
options: “As speech competitors, we should...”
“As an advisory committee, we should consider...”

communication.q: You are noting another speaker’s important point.
options: Keep typing without looking up.
Write briefly and look up frequently.
communication.feedback: Note-taking and visible listening work together.

strategies.title: Continue assertively
strategies.meaning: Continue a brief point when voices overlap.
strategies.risk: Repeatedly talking over others can appear domineering.
strategies.example: “Let me finish this connection briefly, and then I’d like to hear other perspectives.”

strategies.title: Request to go first
strategies.meaning: Acknowledge the other speaker and ask to make your point first.
strategies.advantage: Preserves an opportunity while recognizing another person.
strategies.risk: Repeated requests can control the floor. Honor the promised next turn.
strategies.example: “Would you mind if I finish this point first? I’d like to hear you afterward.”

strategies.title: Yield and request the next turn
strategies.meaning: Let the other person go first, then ask to contribute.
strategies.risk: The discussion may move on before your point fits.
strategies.example: “Go ahead. I’d like to build on that afterward.”

strategies.title: Claim a direct connection
strategies.meaning: Explain why your point responds immediately to the previous speaker.
strategies.risk: Repeated urgency claims can dominate the floor.
strategies.example: “Could I respond briefly to that concern before we change topics?”

speaking.title: Simultaneous start
speaking.q: You and Avery start speaking together. You have spoken often; Avery has not.
options: Talk louder without acknowledging Avery.
“Go ahead, Avery. I have a related point to share afterward.”
Say your idea is more important.
feedback: This risks dominating someone with fewer turns.
This supports participation while preserving your opportunity.

speaking.title: Direct response
speaking.q: Jordan raises a concern your research addresses, but someone else also wants to speak.
options: “Could I respond briefly with a relevant finding, then hear the next perspective?”
Ignore them and speak at length.
Never speak if anyone else wants a turn.
feedback: This explains the connection and acknowledges others.
Relevant research still needs collaborative delivery.
Withholding useful evidence can hinder the group.

speaking.title: Cut off mid-sentence
speaking.q: Your voice fades and another student begins before you finish.
options: Stop participating.
Argue over them.
“I’d like to finish this thought, then hear your point.” Finish briefly and yield.
feedback: Escalation does not resolve the speaking order.
This preserves your turn while respecting the other speaker.

options: “Let’s talk about something else.”
“Building on Maya and Jordan, we could evaluate a small transportation pilot before a larger investment, examining cost and access together.”
“We are almost out of time.”
applications.feedback: This synthesizes ideas into a possible solution.

options: “Sam has spoken, so no one else should.”
“Could we evaluate transportation and communication proposals, then choose final recommendations with our remaining time?”
“I will make the final decision.”
applications.feedback: This supports the deliverable without taking control from the group.

options: “Begin the next item.”
“Five minutes remain.”
“Combining the proposals could address cost and accessibility.”
“Could we hear someone else?”
questions.explanation: Connecting ideas develops a possible solution.

options: Share every statistic regardless of topic.
Cite publication and date, explain the finding, and connect it to the discussion.
Replace evidence with stories.
Repeat a point for the judge.
questions.explanation: Relevant, cited, explained evidence supports problem-solving.

questions.q: How can you invite someone who has contributed little?
options: Repeatedly call on them by name.
Ignore participation.
At a transition, invite any additional perspectives.
Criticize quiet participants.
questions.explanation: A broad invitation avoids putting one person on the spot.

questions.q: Why maintain volume through a sentence ending?
options: It guarantees no interruption.
It helps others hear the complete thought and recognize the turn is not over.
It establishes leadership.
It avoids listening.
questions.explanation: Clear endings help turn-taking, particularly in noisy rooms.

questions.q: You have spoken frequently while another student has not. You start together. What is generally strongest?
options: Talk over them.
Declare your idea more important.
Yield and ask to share your point afterward.
Stop participating entirely.
questions.explanation: Yielding balances participation while keeping a future opportunity.

1.q: “We discussed three solutions: extended program hours, transportation support, and better advertising.”
why: This summarizes proposals already discussed without developing a new recommendation.
This lists existing ideas but does not connect them into a new direction.
This is substantive: it restates proposals, rather than managing the process.

1.q: “If we combine Avery's outreach proposal with Maya's transportation pilot, we could test whether awareness and access need to improve together.”
why: It goes beyond restating ideas by proposing a combined test.
This credits two ideas and develops a combined approach.
This develops the group's thinking, rather than managing procedure.

1.q: “We have six minutes remaining. Should we move to our final recommendations?”
why: It doesn't recap any findings.
It doesn't develop a new substantive insight.
This manages the group's process and time.

1.q: “Our main concern was affordability. We agreed to recommend a small pilot and review its costs before expansion.”
why: This restates the group's concern and agreed recommendation.
It reports a decision rather than forming a new connection.
It describes substantive findings rather than procedure.

1.q: “Jordan raised the cost issue, and Sam suggested a phased approach. Combining those ideas, we could make cost reviews a requirement before each phase expands.”
why: The speaker adds a new requirement, not just a recap.
It credits existing ideas and combines them into a developed recommendation.
This is substantive reasoning, not process management.

2.q: Which combination creates the clearest new direction?
a: Repeat Maya's transportation idea without addressing the others.
Combine transportation access, cost controls, communication, and a pilot into a coordinated recommendation.
Select whichever idea was mentioned most often.
why: Repeating one idea overlooks the other viewpoints.
This combines proposals and concerns into a possible implementation strategy.
Frequency alone does not establish the best solution.

3.q: Which is the strongest final summary?
a: Everyone contributed good ideas, and I think we solved the task.

Our group identified transportation, affordability, and communication barriers. We agreed to recommend a limited pilot combining transportation assistance and outreach, with evaluation before expansion. We still need to clarify the funding source.
Maya said one thing, Jordan said another, Avery added something, and Sam had another idea.
why: This is too vague and claims success without identifying findings.
This states major issues, the agreed recommendation, and an unresolved question.
This repeats the speaking order without organizing findings.

4.context: Five support a city-funded transportation pilot; two object over costs. The task asks for unanimity.
4.q: What is the most constructive next step?
a: Declare that five votes are enough.
Ask the concerned participants what changes would make the proposal acceptable.
Ignore objections and move to the summary.
why: A majority does not resolve objections when seeking unanimity.
Understanding concerns opens a path to negotiation.
Ignoring concerns prevents meaningful consensus.

4.context: The two participants could support the pilot if initial costs are limited.
a: Propose a limited pilot with a spending cap and evaluation before expansion.
Your concerns are holding everyone back.
why: This addresses the concern while retaining the proposal.
Criticism makes negotiation harder.
A workable compromise deserves consideration first.

4.context: A possible compromise has emerged, but only two minutes remain.
a: Begin an extended debate on unrelated alternatives.
State the revised recommendation and ask whether substantial concerns remain.
why: This distracts from a timely decision.
A focused check tests whether the compromise is supported.
Silence alone does not establish support.

5.q: Which required element is least developed?
why: The transportation pilot addresses access.
The social media campaign addresses communication.
The proposal does not explain how it remains affordable.

5.q: Which revision most directly addresses the gap?
a: Add a spending cap, identify potential funding, and evaluate costs before expansion.
Ask whether everyone thinks the task is solved.
why: These add concrete affordability considerations.
Confidence does not fill a missing requirement.
A vague question does not repair the proposal.

5.q: Which closing question is most useful?
a: Does everyone think we did a good job?
Does our revised proposal address access, communication, and affordability realistically, and can we all support it?
why: This asks for an impression, not a task audit.
This checks requirements and invites meaningful confirmation.
This asks about timing rather than the deliverable.

6.q: The round ends as the judge prepares the ballot. What should you do?
why: Lingering interferes with the judge's responsibilities.
Leaving promptly respects the judge and schedule.
The judge should not be pressed for rankings.

6.q: The judge offers unsolicited verbal feedback. What is best?
a: Politely conclude, leave, and consult your coach.
why: Your coach can determine whether follow-up is appropriate.
Students should not confront judges.
A prolonged critique at the table is inappropriate.

a: You made a thoughtful point about costs. I appreciated that perspective.
Our group would have been better without some ideas.
The judge clearly preferred my contributions.
why: Specific, sincere recognition builds relationships.
Criticizing others undermines professionalism.
Claiming a judge's preference is inappropriate.

7.q: Which contribution best connects the viewpoints?
a: Maya had the best idea, so let's use that.
Building on Maya's transportation proposal, Jordan's cost concern, and Avery's communication idea, we could recommend a limited pilot paired with outreach and a cost review.
why: This discards other perspectives.
It credits multiple contributors and coordinates their ideas.
It does not develop a recommendation.

7.q: Which summary accurately represents the proposed direction?
a: We discussed possibilities and the problem matters.
Our proposed plan combines transportation assistance and improved outreach, with an initial pilot and cost evaluation before expansion.
We solved every problem affecting teen participation.
why: This omits the actual proposed outcome.
This identifies components without exaggeration.
This claims more than the proposal establishes.

7.q: Jordan still wants a clear spending limit. What should the group do?
a: Add a spending cap and check whether it addresses the concern.
Ignore Jordan because the others agree.
why: This addresses the remaining objection and supports consensus.
A majority does not erase a meaningful concern.
Support remains unconfirmed.

7.q: Which closing question best evaluates the proposal?
a: Does our revised proposal address access, communication, and affordability, and can everyone support it?
why: This asks for a general impression.
This checks requirements and group support.
Speaking time is not the final task audit.

a: Combine viewpoints into a new insight or recommendation.
why: That is a chronological recap.
Synthesis uses connections to advance thinking.
That is procedural.
Popularity alone is not synthesis.

8.q: What makes a final summary effective?
a: Focus only on your own ideas.
Organize findings, accurately identify agreements, and credit contributors.
why: A summary should be concise.
It represents the group's work.
It also distinguishes agreements from unresolved concerns.
Review is needed before claiming completion.

8.q: A unanimous recommendation is needed, but two participants object. What next?
why: A majority is not unanimity.
Consensus requires addressing concerns.
Their objections still matter.
This leaves the disagreement unresolved.

8.q: How should the group check task completion?
a: Assume the final minutes mean success.
Compare the proposal against the required problem and deliverable components.
why: Enjoyment is not a task criterion.
Time elapsed does not establish completion.
A task-focused review reveals missing requirements.
Speaking order does not evaluate the deliverable.

8.q: The judge offers unsolicited performance comments. What should you do?
a: Respond politely, leave, and consult your coach.
why: Do not confront judges.
Do not solicit rankings.
A coach can determine appropriate follow-up.
Avoid extending the interaction at the table.

notes: Maya: Transportation barriers prevent some students from attending.
Jordan: The group should consider program costs.
Avery: Students need clearer information about opportunities.
Lack of awareness is a communication barrier.
Sam: A pilot could test the proposal before expansion.
A pilot is a proposed implementation approach.
All: Recommend a limited pilot combining transportation assistance and outreach.
This explicitly identifies the agreed recommendation.
All: What funding source would support the pilot?
Funding remains unresolved; do not present it as settled.

2: I connected at least two viewpoints.
I credited the people whose ideas I used.
I added a new insight or recommendation.
My language is collaborative and professional.
7: I credited at least two participants.
I connected ideas rather than just listing them.
I addressed access, communication, and affordability.
I invited confirmation or identified an unresolved concern.
My language was concise, respectful, and professional.
